items.title: Grand Canyon’s South Rim hotels to reopen as park eases water restrictions
items.summary: GRAND CANYON NATIONAL PARK, Ariz. (AP) — Officials at Grand Canyon National Park announced Wednesday that they are easing water restrictions, meaning hotels on the South Rim will once again be able to accommodate overnight guests. The famous El Tovar Hotel along with several other lodges will reopen Friday now that the park has reached a milestone in restoration of water service following severe flooding earlier this year. Flooding in late August caused three deaths, prompted rescues and damaged key infrastructure, including a water intake pump and a significant stretch of a decades-old pipeline that supplied water for millions of visitors to the South Rim and about 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village. At the time, officials said they were just over a month away from completing a more than $200 million upgrade to the 12.5-mile-long (20-kilometer) Transcanyon Waterline. More flooding in September damaged temporary repairs. Although lodging is reopening, park officials urge visitors to conserve as restoration of the water system continues. “Simple actions, including taking shorter showers, turning off faucets when not in use and avoiding unnecessary water use, help support the park’s water system as operations resume,” the park said in its announcement. Food and beverage services will resume gradually, according to park officials. By Associated Press Banner image: The Grand Canyon. Image courtesy of Amy Martin via National Park Service. This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Grand Canyon’s South Rim hotels to reopen as park eases water restrictions

items.title: UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds
items.summary:
Populations at lowest level on record with 45% of native breeding species in decline, environment watchdog says

The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, her ministers and Natural England are breaking the law by failing to intervene to slow the “deeply concerning” decline of Britain’s wild birds, the UK’s environment regulator has said.

New data shows that wild bird populations have dropped to their lowest level on record, with almost half – 45% – of 132 native breeding species in decline over a five-year period.

items.title: Bhutan wins $1.3m Earthshot Prize for maintaining 70% forest cover
items.summary: Bhutan has been crowned one of the 2026 winners of the Earthshot Prize for its work in conserving Himalayan forests, receiving 1 million pounds, or about $1.3 million, to scale up its national landscape restoration efforts. Bhutan, a Himalayan kingdom of 800,000 people, was recognized in the “Protect and Restore Nature” category for writing nature protection into its national constitution and safeguarding vital headwaters, according to an Earthshot Prize announcement. The country maintains nearly 70% forest cover — surpassing its constitutional requirement of at least 60% — and is the world’s first carbon-negative nation. Its forests protect Himalayan freshwater systems that sustain 1.6 billion people downstream across South Asia, generating an estimated $14.5 billion in annual ecosystem services, according to data cited by prize organizers. “In Bhutan, protecting nature has always been part of who we are,” Princess Chimi Yangzom Wangchuck, daughter of the fourth king of Bhutan, said in a video released by the Earthshot Prize. “Protecting nature is part of our national responsibility. It is not just a promise; it is the law.” The prize money will accelerate “Restore Bhutan,” a national initiative launched in 2025 to restore 50,000 hectares (nearly 124,000 acres) of degraded forests, farmlands, and urban landscapes by 2030, according to an emailed press release by the Earthshot Prize. The initiative aims to sequester 1.96 million metric tons of carbon dioxide and secure 133 billion liters (35 billion gallons) of water. “Change is not only possible. It is already happening,”…
items.t: Bhutan wins $1.3m Earthshot Prize for maintaining 70% forest cover

items.title: Indigenous communities in Panama fear a second dam as damage from first goes unrepaired
items.summary: Nearly two decades after construction began on the CHAN-75 hydroelectric dam project, Indigenous Ngäbe communities in western Panama continue to face severe environmental, cultural and spiritual impacts, according to a new report by the Indigenous rights organization Cultural Survival. It found that communities still suffer from displacement, pollution, the loss of local fish species, medicinal plants, spiritual practices and other threats to their livelihoods. As communities continue to fight for reparations, Panamanian authorities have granted a concession for a second dam on the same river. Ismael Quintero, a Ngäbe leader of the Guayabal community, said their lives changed completely when the state-owned electric power generation company Empresa de Generación Eléctrica (EGESA) began to build the first dam in 2007. “Crops were abundant, and there was free navigation along the Changuinola River,” he told Mongabay via WhatsApp voice messages. “Our whole family enjoyed the clean and healthy river at that time.” For the Ngäbe people, the river traditionally holds deep spiritual and cultural significance. Quintero said it provides them with food, such as fish and shrimp, and serves as a source of inspiration and strength. It is sacred to them, he added. They traditionally believe that a spirit — the owner of the fish and river ecosystems — resides within it, and therefore, any catch is a gift from this spirit. For this reason, they offer prayers to the spirit before undertaking any activities there. Tilapia fish caught in the Changuinola River by a member of a Ngäbe…
items.t: Indigenous communities in Panama fear a second dam as damage from first goes unrepaired

items.title: 50 Backyard Wildlife Photos That Prove You Don’t Have To Go Far To Find Nature, Shared Online
items.summary:
Wildlife photography is usually associated with remote places: savannas, rainforests, frozen tundras, and photographers who travel thousands of miles for a single frame. But some of the most memorable encounters with wild animals don’t require a passport or a long lens. They happen just past the back door, on a fence post, beneath a bird feeder, or at the edge of a lawn as the light starts to fade. 

These moments are easy to miss. A backyard visitor rarely announces itself, and it rarely stays long. It might appear for a few seconds while the coffee is brewing or slip through the garden at dusk when no one is watching. Catching it on camera takes the same things any wildlife photographer relies on: patience, a quiet presence, and the instinct to grab the camera before the moment disappears. 

National Geographic, a name synonymous with extraordinary wildlife photography for more than a century, recently turned its attention closer to home. In a post on Threads, the brand invited its followers to show the wildlife they’ve spotted in their own backyards, and people responded in force. The replies quickly filled with photos of wild neighbors captured from porches, gardens, and windows, each one a reminder that nature doesn’t stop at the city limits or the property line. 

Below are 50 of the best photos people shared under National Geographic’s post; take a look.  

More info: threads.com

items.title: ‘Huge experiment in biogeography’: US offshore windfarms are creating artificial reefs
items.summary:
Scientists and fishers study how these ‘reefs’ and the creatures living on them are transforming the ocean floor – and what it means for the fishing industry

A few years ago, Tony DiLernia, a New York-based charter boat captain, heard rumors of prime fishing near the Block Island windfarm, off the tip of Long Island. So he went with his family to see for himself. Almost immediately after motoring up to one of the project’s five turbines, black sea bass and summer flounder started nibbling at his rod and reel.

DiLernia, who has fished for 50 years, wasn’t surprised: he knew about the reef effect, where certain species cluster around structures like the turbines. “It’s what we call ‘stupid fishing’,” he joked. “You’ve got this thousand-foot [signpost] sticking up out of the water saying: ‘Fish here.’”

items.t: ‘Huge experiment in biogeography’: US offshore windfarms are creating artificial reefs

items.title: Study maps jaguars across the Americas to help their populations rebound
items.summary: Residents of a neighborhood in Foz do Iguaçu, in southern Brazil, alerted authorities after spotting a jaguar (Panthera onca) roaming the streets in June 2026. One family was even more surprised when, one morning, they heard a loud commotion and found the animal on their porch. Following a major mobilization involving police, environmental agencies and organizations specializing in the species, the male jaguar was sedated and temporarily taken to a wildlife refuge. A few weeks later, the animal, named Tape’ỹ — a word meaning “the one who lost his way” in the Indigenous Tupi-Guarani language — was released into Iguaçu National Park, near where he had been found. “Jaguars need large areas of habitat to survive. And it’s not enough for these areas to exist: They must be connected, allowing animals to move around, find mates and maintain gene flow between different populations,” says Yara de Melo Barros, executive director of the Onças do Iguaçu Project, one of the organizations involved in Tape’ỹ’s rescue and release. Iguaçu is part of the so-called Green Corridor, which crosses the Brazil-Argentina border and is home to about one-third of the fewer than 300 jaguars still surviving in the Atlantic Forest. It is an important habitat for the species, but highly fragmented and almost completely cut off from the rest of the biome, according to the most comprehensive assessment to date of connectivity across the jaguar’s range throughout the Americas, recently published in the journal Global Change Biology. Tape’ỹ being examined after his rescue…This article was originally…
items.t: Study maps jaguars across the Americas to help their populations rebound

items.title: Better data can help restore Himalayan ecosystems & prepare for climate risks (commentary)
items.summary: In less than seven weeks, two major flood events impacted Nepal’s Himalaya, where ecologically rich mountain landscapes are closely connected to the rivers, forests and floodplains. On the morning of Aug. 26, 2026, a catastrophic flood began with a rock and ice collapse on the northern flank of Langtang Lirung, within Langtang National Park. The park is one of country’s major Himalayan protected areas and provides habitat for species like Himalayan musk deer (Moschus leucogaster), Asiatic black bear (Ursus thibetanus), red panda (Ailurus fulgens) and clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa). Then, on Oct. 11, another destructive flood occurred in the Budhi Gandaki basin after a landslide blocked the river near Chumchet village in Gorkha District within the Manaslu Conservation Area that supports snow leopard (Panthera uncia), musk deer, blue sheep (Pseudois nayaur) and Himalayan tahr (Hemitragus jemlahicus), along with more than 200 recorded Himalayan plant species. While the human cost of these disasters and the damage to physical infrastructure have been reported extensively, much less attention has gone to what they are doing to ecosystems and wildlife in the region. In the Himalaya, because of the extraordinary diversity and interconnectedness, any disturbance created in a high mountain valley can affect forests, wetlands and floodplains much further downstream. Some of the immediate effects are already visible after the recent events, but their ecological and longer-term consequences require systematic assessment. Research on earlier Himalayan disasters shows that major…
items.t: Better data can help restore Himalayan ecosystems & prepare for climate risks (commentary)

items.title: Lucio Usobiaga wins 2026 ‘Nobel Prize of Gastronomy’ for protecting Mexico’s chinampas ecosystem
items.summary: Lucio Usobiaga of Mexico won the 2026 Basque Culinary World Prize for his project Arca Tierra, a network of farmers and the culinary community of Mexico that helps preserve Mexico City’s traditional chinampa agricultural system. The chinampas are an ancient, pre-Aztec series of agricultural canal islands, where small artificial plots of land were built in the wetlands of Xochimilco, in the southern valley of Mexico City. Traditional farmers known as chinamperos still practice this form of agriculture, growing flowers, maize, legumes, and several types of vegetables, Mongabay’s Aimee Gabay reported in 2024. The Basque Culinary World Prize, also referred to as the “Nobel Prize of Gastronomy,” was created in 2016 by the government of the Basque autonomous region in Spain and the Basque Culinary Center, and awards 100,000 euros (about $110,000) to a project chosen by the winner. Arca Tierra cultivates 6 hectares (about 15 acres) within the chinampas and works with 50 farming families across Xochimilco, Puebla, Hidalgo, and the state of Mexico. These farms supply around 60 restaurants in Mexico City with fresh produce.  According to Food & Wine magazine, the chinampa soil’s high organic matter from lake sediments also gives food grown there a special flavor. “I can tell, like from the first bite, when I’m eating a beet from the chinampas,” Usobiaga told Food & Wine.  Usobiaga told Mongabay by email that he wants people to know the chinampero farmers have been living in the chinampas for millennia, and that their important work has mostly gone unseen.  “Mexico City’s future is…
items.t: Lucio Usobiaga wins 2026 ‘Nobel Prize of Gastronomy’ for protecting Mexico’s chinampas ecosystem

items.title: Wildlife trafficking persists in West, Central Africa despite crackdowns: Report
items.summary: At his storefront in Lagos’s sprawling Lekki Craft Market, alongside handwoven raffia baskets and Ankara fabrics, an illegal wildlife trader, identified only as Mr. X, sells an array of carved ivory products. It’s from this shop that he established links with buyers across Asia, sending out large volumes of wildlife products sourced from the forests of Gabon, Cameroon, and the Central African Republic. In early 2022, Mr. X was arrested for unlawful possession of nearly 900 kilograms (nearly 2,000 pounds) of pangolin scales and 145 kg (320 lb) of elephant ivory. His operations ceased, and in May 2023, he was convicted and sentenced to two years in prison. But within months, Mr. X was free. Some 18 months later, investigators found that he was once again offering up pangolin scales for sale. Business had rebounded. Investigators found that Mr. X had likely spent only a few months in custody and reportedly paid several million naira, the equivalent of a few thousand U.S. dollars, in bribes through his lawyer during court proceedings. The saga of Mr. X is emblematic of the ongoing corruption and persistence of West and Central Africa’s illegal wildlife trade that’s pushing many species to the brink, despite better enforcement in recent years, according to a new report by the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), an international NGO that digs into environmental crimes across the world. Criminal networks, investigators found, have continued to evolve and evade efforts to clamp down on the flow of products derived from imperiled wildlife.…This article was originally…
items.t: Wildlife trafficking persists in West, Central Africa despite crackdowns: Report

items.title: Country diary: Thrilling views of Iceland’s humpbacks, (perhaps) lured in by Céline Dion | Claire Stares
items.summary:
Eyjafjörður: Our boat was surrounded by around 15 of them, exploding their exhalations out of the water – and numbers are increasing here

For the first half-hour, Eyjafjörður, Iceland’s longest fjord, offered few signs of marine life – just three cormorants and a raft of common eiders. Then, suddenly, there it was. A distant spout of water vapour. A humpback whale.

As we motored out, more bushy plumes appeared to port and starboard, until we found the boat surrounded by about 15 individuals. Cutting the engine, the captain announced that he was about to employ a secret technique to coax the whales closer. There were raised eyebrows as the opening notes of Céline Dion’s My Heart Will Go On crackled over the speakers. But, as if on cue, two explosive exhalations erupted alongside the boat, prompting whoops of delight.

Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.

items.title: Rare encounter with isolated Indigenous Awá people in Brazil exposes vulnerability
items.summary: On Nov. 16, a group of roughly 20 Indigenous Awá people living in voluntary isolation approached an Indigenous Guajajara village, in Brazil’s northeastern Maranhão state. The rare encounter has mobilized Indigenous peoples and activists concerned about the safety of the Awá, considered the most threatened group on the planet. The motivation for the unusual interaction is unclear, but Guajajara leaders “expressed concern about the physical condition of some members of the group, especially children and older people, who appeared to be very thin,” according to accounts and images posted on social media by Indigenous organizations. The Guajajara reportedly offered the Awá food and other objects; the Awá remained there briefly before returning to the forest. Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, told Mongabay by email that technical teams are monitoring the situation and that it had activated a contingency plan to “ensure that the relevant agencies are prepared to respond appropriately to any developments in the situation, especially regarding the ethno-environmental protection, health and safety of the Indigenous people involved.” Funai added that the peoples’ right to self-determination would continue to be respected. Unlike other isolated peoples who make frequent contact, this is the first time in decades that the Awá of the Arariboia Indigenous Territory “have appeared in this way and made such close contact with other people,” Sarah Shenker, director and senior researcher at the Indigenous rights organization Survival International Brazil, told Mongabay by phone.…
items.t: Rare encounter with isolated Indigenous Awá people in Brazil exposes vulnerability

items.title: Jason Clay, who persuaded big business to help save nature, has died at 75
items.summary: In 1988 Jason Clay attended a Grateful Dead concert at Madison Square Garden and met a man who wanted to help save tropical rainforests. Clay, an anthropologist who had worked with Indigenous communities, asked what he did for a living. “I make ice cream,” the man replied. It was Ben Cohen of Ben & Jerry’s. Clay suggested developing a flavor using nuts gathered from tropical forests. He thought higher payments for forest products might give people a reason to keep the trees standing. Within a year, Rainforest Crunch was on supermarket shelves. Clay set up a trading company and went on to work with more than 50 businesses on some 200 products, generating roughly $100 million in retail sales. At one point, he said, his operation was buying around a fifth of the world’s Brazil nuts. It paid gatherers two or three times the going rate, and other buyers raised their prices to compete. The people gathering the nuts weren’t generally the ones clearing the forests. Ranchers and loggers had little reason to change what they were doing, and Clay eventually called Rainforest Crunch a failure. “We were attacking the wrong driver,” he explained in a 2010 TED talk. He should have been working on beef, lumber and soy. Clay, who died on November 16th aged 75, spent more than three decades at the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), where he worked to change how major companies bought agricultural commodities linked to deforestation and other environmental problems. items.t: Jason Clay, who persuaded big business to help save nature, has died at 75

items.title: In Zimbabwe, trusted local guardians help communities coexist with lions
items.summary: Conservation biologist and founder of the nonprofit Wildlife Conservation Action, Moreangels Mbizah joins the Mongabay Newscast this week to detail her work helping reduce human-wildlife conflict between African lions and communities in Zimbabwe. The group began working only six years ago in two wards of Nyaminyami rural district, and since then has recorded a 98% reduction in conflict incidents there. Across the districts of Mbire and Binga, conflict has decreased by 53%. To accomplish this, WCA has pioneered a “community guardian” model. Known as “Batabilili,” these guardians are trained by the organization and implement a range of mitigation measures, including helping farmers secure livestock in above-ground kraals, monitoring lion movement, and conducting community meetings. “They are trusted because they come from these communities, and they are their children, their brothers and sisters,” Mbizah says. “They are part of the community fabric, so that makes it really important in terms of the buy-in and the ideas and the decisions that are being made when it comes to lion conservation.” She says this has also helped reduce retaliatory killings of lions for preying on livestock, because community members’ concerns are directly addressed by a trusted member. “There’s no one that is supporting them when they incur these losses. No one comes to see and to support, to provide … emotional or psychological support when a conflict incident happen[s]. So we wanted to change that,” Mbizah says. “They always felt that [the] wildlife authority, they care about wildlife and they…
items.t: In Zimbabwe, trusted local guardians help communities coexist with lions

items.title: Prince William’s presents Earthshot Prize winners with $1.3M each in Mumbai
items.summary: MUMBAI, India (AP) — Prince William presented five Earthshot Prize winners with 1 million pounds ($1.3 million) each on Tuesday, recognizing their efforts to tackle the world’s climate challenges. The annual ceremony, held this year in Mumbai, marked the centerpiece of William and Princess Catherine’s three-day visit to India. The Earthshot Prize winners were selected from 15 finalists for their work in areas ranging from clean transport and renewable energy to forest conservation and marine protection. Four were Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, for its electric transport initiatives; PFAS-Free France, for its campaign to ban toxic “forever chemicals”; Niue Ocean Wide Trust, for protecting marine ecosystems; and Ørsted, for advancing offshore wind energy. The fifth recipient was the country of Bhutan for its work in conserving Himalayan forests. William, the Prince of Wales, established the prize through his Royal Foundation in 2020 to encourage inventors and entrepreneurs to develop technologies to combat global warming and mitigate its effects. The ceremony at Mumbai’s Jio World Convention Centre brought together Bollywood celebrities, innovators, entrepreneurs and environmental advocates. William and the Princess of Wales, commonly known as Kate, began their visit Monday. The couple have played street cricket in Mumbai, ridden in an electric rickshaw and met leading figures from India’s cricket, fashion and film industries. They are scheduled to meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday. The trip marks a significant step in Kate’s return to overseas royal…
items.t: Prince William’s presents Earthshot Prize winners with $1.3M each in Mumbai

items.title: The scimitar-horned oryx is back in Chad
items.summary: The scimitar-horned oryx, an antelope with a majestic set of sword-like horns, had disappeared from Chad by the late 1980s and was declared extinct in the wild globally in 2000. But now, thanks to a reintroduction program led by the NGO Sahara Conservation, its conservation status has improved to “endangered.” The oryx population in Ouadi Rimé–Ouadi Achim Wildlife Reserve, Chad’s largest protected area, has grown from 25 individuals in 2016 to 700 today. That makes it the largest herd in the world. However, the species continues to face challenges, including climate change impacts such as prolonged droughts and shifting conditions, as well as competition from livestock for grazing lands.This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: The scimitar-horned oryx is back in Chad

items.title: In final stretch of climate summit, Indigenous leaders call for lasting action
items.summary: The annual U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change gathering drew historic levels of Indigenous attendance in Belém, Brazil, last year, leading some to dub it “the Indigenous COP.” But the event was marked by frustration and protest, with many Indigenous leaders calling it little more than a continuation of a long-standing pattern of exclusion from international negotiations. This year’s gathering in Antalya, Türkiye, is billed as an “implementation” conference focused less on sweeping new pledges than on the procedural work of turning previous agreements into action. For Indigenous advocates, that makes this climate summit (known as COP31), which runs from Nov. 9 until Nov. 20, a test of whether the promises made last year translate into tangible changes, including greater authority over climate action. “It is still a struggle,” said Edward Porokwa, who is Maasai and a member of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues. “I’m yet to really determine whether there will be any more progress that is made in terms of realization of the rights of Indigenous people.” Indigenous advocates are pressing governments to follow through on their commitments to secure and strengthen Indigenous land rights on about 161 million hectares (400 million acres) in tropical forest countries; effectively provide $1.8 billion in funding; and respect rights to free, prior, and informed consent in the energy transition. Despite those pledges and wins hitting an international finance target, some climate funds have been slow to reach affected communities, and Indigenous land…
items.t: In final stretch of climate summit, Indigenous leaders call for lasting action

items.title: Why conservation needs independent journalism (commentary)
items.summary: In 2021, we received a tip from a source in Sabah, Malaysia, about a proposed carbon credit deal. We received this tip because we’d developed a relationship with the source over 15 years. They trusted us to protect their identity and verify what they gave us. And if we covered it, they knew the information would reach the people it needed to reach. The reporting would also enable local outlets in Malaysia to pursue the story because they could deflect blame to Mongabay for breaking the news. The deal was a big one. It covered some 2 million hectares (5 million acres) of rainforest in the state of Sabah in Malaysian Borneo. But that was only part of the story. The more troubling issue was that a group of senior Sabah officials was negotiating with a Singapore company incorporated just two years earlier with only $1,000 in paid-up capital and no demonstrated track record of managing a conservation project on anything approaching this scale. Indigenous communities whose customary rights could be affected had not been meaningfully consulted. Their ancestral land was potentially being locked up in an opaque contract with largely unknown operators for more than a century. When the story broke, it immediately made headlines in Malaysia and beyond. The timing was important. A Malaysian delegation had been planning to market the project’s carbon credits to investors at the U.N. climate conference in Glasgow, Scotland. Those plans fell apart. Back in Malaysia, Indigenous leader Adrian Lasimbang took the government…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Why conservation needs independent journalism (commentary)

items.title: Another Sri Lankan leopard caught in a snare. These big cats need protecting, experts say
items.summary: COLOMBO — The stillness of a cold November night at Athad Tea Estate in Norwood in Sri Lanka’s Central Highlands was suddenly shattered by agonizing growls. Awakened by the cries echoing through the darkness, estate workers rushed to check, only to find the horrifying sight of a leopard (Panthera pardus kotiya) caught in a wire snare, writhing desperately to break free from the tightening trap. The trapped animal was a female, approximately 3.5 years old. The wire had severely compressed her flank as she relentlessly struggled to free herself. Officers from the Department of Wildlife Conservation’s (DWC), accompanied by a veterinarian from the veterinary unit at Randenigala, reached the location early morning and anesthetized the agitated animal. Although the compression was severe, she had fortunately escaped major external cut wounds which is common in snared victims, said Akalanka Pinidiya, the veterinarian in charge of the Central Region. Even when the leopard appears to be calm, wildlife officers do not release snared leopards immediately. “When a leopard gets caught in a snare, its struggle to escape can cause serious internal injuries, particularly to organs such as the kidneys, which can prove fatal even though not visible,” said Pinidiya, who has treated a number of such snared leopards. According to the wildlife vet, this leopard is passing feces and urine, and she has even eaten a small portion of meat provided. “These are encouraging signs that there are no serious internal damages, but the leopard will remain under observation for a few…This article was…
items.t: Another Sri Lankan leopard caught in a snare. These big cats need protecting, experts say

items.title: Everyday Dog Walks Could Become An Early Warning System For Invasive Plants, Scientists Say
items.summary:
For centuries, people have relied on dogs’ noses to do what human senses can’t. Hunters used scent hounds to track game through forests, truffle hunters in Italy bred dogs to find fungi buried underground, and today dogs help find explosives, drugs, and even signs of some diseases. Now, scientists in Germany have given them a new kind of target: invasive plants.

More info: journals.plos.org | youtube.com 

Dogs are being trained to detect invasive plants before they spread and threaten local ecosystems 

Doğan Alpaslan Demir/Pexels 

Researchers from the Helmholtz Center for Environmental Research (UFZ) in Leipzig set out to test whether ordinary pet dogs and their owners could be trained to find invasive plant species in the wild. The results were encouraging. In a final field test, the volunteer teams located their target plants with an average success rate of 75%. The findings were published in the scientific journal PLOS ONE in November 2026. 

Invasive species may not get as much attention as climate change, but their impact is enormous. According to a 2023 global assessment by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES), invasive species have been a major factor in 60% of recorded plant and animal extinctions, and they cost the world more than $423 billion in 2019 alone. Once an invasive plant takes hold, it can spread rapidly, crowd out native species, and change the habitats wildlife depends on. 

German researchers tested whether ordinary pet dogs could help ecologists track three invasive species 

Александр…
items.t: Pet Dogs Trained By German Scientists Found Invasive Plants In The Wild With 75% Success

items.title: Three-legged Persian leopard’s 150-mile journey highlights Caucasus border hazards
items.summary: An endangered Persian leopard that researchers have named Aren recently completed a 240-kilometer (150-mile) journey through the snow-bound Caucasus Mountains that straddle Russia, Georgia, Armenia, and Azerbaijan. Aren not just navigated a landscape that still contains decades-old minefields from prior conflicts, but he did so on just three legs. His journey highlights the severe hazards that border minefields and fencing pose to wildlife, Mongabay contributor Kayleigh Long told host Mike DiGirolamo on a recent episode of the Mongabay newscast. Persian leopards (Panthera pardus tulliana) are endangered, with fewer than 1,044 individuals remaining worldwide, according to the IUCN, the global wildlife conservation authority. In the past two decades, scientists have documented just three leopard sightings in Georgia and 10 in Armenia. Long’s reporting for Mongabay highlighted Aren’s trek, which was first identified by camera traps in Armenia’s Arpa Protected Area. He started off as a healthy four-legged male, but when rangers spotted him months later, the lower part of his left foreleg was missing — an injury Arpa rangers say may have been inflicted by an antipersonnel mine along the border of Nakhchivan, an Azerbaijani exclave. Such injuries are common in the region. According to WWF Armenia, three of the 10 leopards recorded in Armenia since 2002 have lost a limb. Soviet-era electric signal fences known as Sistema, along with modern border barriers, further obstruct movement across Iran, Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia. “Leopards do not recognize political boundaries,”…
items.t: Three-legged Persian leopard’s 150-mile journey highlights Caucasus border hazards

items.title: Meet The Orangutan Who Adopted A Starving Stray Hound And Turned Him Into His Best Friend At First Hug
items.summary:
Sometime in the mid-2000s, at a wildlife park in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, a young orangutan named Suryia was on his way to the river with an elephant when a skinny stray hound trotted out of the trees. Suryia climbed down, ran straight over and started playing with the newcomer on the spot.

The dog was Roscoe, a bluetick coonhound nobody ever came looking for. He stayed. Within a few years, photos of the two friends had reached Oprah’s studio, a National Geographic series, a children’s book and one of the most-shared ads on the internet.

Suryia was riding an elephant down to the river when a skinny stray hound wandered out of the woods 

sarcastic_desert_ferret 

Suryia was born at The Institute of Greatly Endangered and Rare Species, better known as Myrtle Beach Safari. He worked there as an animal ambassador, helping staff raise baby primates. One day he was heading to the water on the back of Bubbles the elephant when a painfully thin bluetick coonhound bounded out of the trees. Instead of keeping his distance, the young ape slid down and threw his arms around the newcomer, and within minutes the two were rolling in the grass. Park founder Bhagavan “Doc” Antle later recalled that the dog “looked really thin and a little lost,” so the team fed him. Roscoe repaid the kindness by following them straight through the gate.

Nobody ever claimed Roscoe, so he moved in and became Suryia’s full-time walking, swimming and wrestling partner 

sarcastic_desert_ferret 

sarcastic_desert_ferret 

Staff called around looking for an…
items.t: Meet Suryia And Roscoe, The Orangutan And Stray Hound Who Became Inseparable At First Hug

items.title: Global clean energy transition demands millions of acres, threatening indigenous rights: Report
items.summary: The global push to transition away from fossil fuels is driving a massive surge in mineral extraction and renewable energy infrastructure that is fundamentally reorganizing land use, resource flows and geopolitical power relations, according to a recent report. The report, published in November by global nonprofit the International Land Coalition (ILC) and the Land Matrix, a land monitoring initiative, reveals that commercial concessions for clean energy and critical transition minerals now span an estimated 328 million hectares (about 810.5 million acres) globally — an area equivalent to the size of India. “What is most striking, and genuinely surprising, is that despite relentless global calls to accelerate and ‘fast-track’ the energy transition, until now, we simply did not know the true scale of its physical land footprint,” Jérémy Bourgoin, the report co-author who leads the ILC Knowledge & Research team, told Mongabay by email. Projects in early exploration and planning phases account for 80% of the total mapped area. “Perhaps the most sobering takeaway is the sheer scale of what is yet to come,” Bourgoin said. “The acute social, environmental, and territorial impacts documented in the report reflect a landscape where only roughly 20% of mapped projects are currently operational.” The report finds that large-scale solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal facilities account for 159 million hectares (393 million acres), while mining concessions for critical minerals like copper, lithium, nickel, and cobalt cover 239 million hectares (591 million acres). Building low-carbon…
items.t: Global clean energy transition demands millions of acres, threatening indigenous rights: Report

items.title: This Page Shares Heartwarming Moments That Prove Cats Have A Special Place In People’s Hearts (26 Pics)
items.summary:
The Facebook page “Love cats” shares touching animal stories from around the world, featuring everything from rescues and acts of generosity to unusual friendships and devoted pets. Each post pairs a photograph with a story about the animal pictured, giving readers a chance to learn more about the circumstances behind these moments. Some stories highlight people going out of their way to help animals in need. A shop owner provides stray cats with a warm place to sleep, a butcher in Turkey makes sure hungry animals get fed, and a firefighter looks after a tiny rescued kitten. Others feature volunteers and everyday people who dedicate their time, money, and energy to caring for animals that might otherwise have nowhere to turn.

Of course, humans aren't the only ones capable of showing kindness and affection. The page also shares stories about the relationships animals develop with each other and with their families. From a cat keeping a baby company to a dog forming an unexpected friendship with a kitten, some of these moments are as adorable as they are touching. Not every story involves a dramatic rescue or an extraordinary act of generosity, either. Sometimes, it's simply about someone noticing an animal that needs help, making room for another pet in their home, or finding a way to make a beloved companion's life a little easier.

We've put together a collection of these heartwarming stories, so scroll down to see the photos and read their accompanying stories below, and let us know which ones touched your heart most.

items.t: This Page Shared 26 Heartwarming Cat Stories That Show How Much Kindness And Love Can Mean

items.title: DRC’s Critical Minerals Moment
items.summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) sits at the center of the global race for the critical minerals needed for advanced technologies ranging from medical equipment and military hardware to electric cars and industrial batteries. As demand accelerates, the country has become a focal point for geopolitical competition over mineral access. In this Special Issue, Mongabay journalists examine how competition for critical minerals is reshaping governance, communities and landscapes in the DRC. From deadly accidents at artisanal mines to international deals, the series explores how conflict, foreign investment and weak oversight intersect in one of the world’s most resource-rich regions.This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: DRC’s Critical Minerals Moment

items.title: Plans for a new marine protected area boost whale shark conservation in Indonesia’s Saleh Bay
items.summary: Plans to create a marine protected area for whale sharks in Indonesia’s Saleh Bay would give the world’s largest fish important new protections across several stages of its lifecycle, conservationists say. Besides serving as a migratory route and feeding ground for adults, there is growing evidence that the sheltered bay acts as a safe haven for juvenile whale sharks (Rhincodon typus), allowing them to develop in waters rich in food but free of predators. Sightings of newborns also indicate the bay may be a whale shark pupping ground, which would make it the first-ever to be documented anywhere in the world, although researchers caution this is yet to be confirmed. According to a document from the provincial government, seen by Mongabay, the marine protected area (MPA) would cover 90% of known whale shark hotspots in Saleh Bay, which lies in the shadow of the volcanic Mount Tambora on Sumbawa Island in West Nusa Tenggara province. The species, classified as endangered by the IUCN, has been monitored there since 2015. The MPA has received the support of the West Nusa Tenggara provincial government and local communities, with conservationists now waiting on a final decision from Jakarta. A whale shark in Saleh Bay, 2016. Besides serving as a migratory route and feeding ground for adults, there is growing evidence that the sheltered bay acts as a safe haven for juvenile whale sharks. Image by Egaryan Saadi via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0). “[The MPA] is important because this bay represents a key…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Plans for a new marine protected area boost whale shark conservation in Indonesia’s Saleh Bay

items.title: Singapore investors hope for diplomatic help after Indonesia halts $50b electricity export push
items.summary: SINGAPORE — With Singapore’s appetite for electricity expected to balloon by as much as half its current peak demand by 2031, the country is turning to its neighbors to pipe in clean power — in part to keep its data centers humming and support the uptake of electric vehicles. The city-state, which has little room to spare for large-scale power generators of virtually any type, has inked agreements to import electricity from Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam, and even as far afield as Australia. Singapore aims to reach net-zero carbon emissions by the middle of the century. In early 2025, the government said it would reduce the contribution of gas to its power-generating mix to 50% by 2035 — down from 95% currently. Singapore’s Energy Market Authority has granted conditional approval to several companies, most recently in 2024, to import a total of 3.4 gigawatts of low-carbon electricity from Indonesia by the middle of the next decade, a quarter of what Singapore estimates it will need by then. Now, those plans hang in the balance after Indonesia said it will not allow them to go ahead. There appears to be an intensifying diplomatic standoff, in part, over haze and energy. Singapore has let its frustration with the transboundary haze from its larger neighbor known. In late October, National Environment Agency publicly called on 10 Singapore-based plantation companies to take action regarding possible fires on their Indonesian concessions. The move came just over a week after Prime Minister Lawrence Wong indicated the…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Singapore investors hope for diplomatic help after Indonesia halts $50b electricity export push

items.title: Thailand-Myanmar river pollution agreement was weakened, then signed. China remains silent
items.summary: MAE SAI, Thailand — Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow made a one-day visit to Naypyidaw, the capital of Myanmar, on Nov. 12 to speak with the military regime about trade, border security and, notably, the pollution of Thai rivers that have been contaminated by mining pollution. While Thailand’s foreign ministry reported that transboundary pollution flowing from mines in Myanmar through rivers into Thailand was discussed, the visit underscored the lack of progress on bilateral solutions to the heavy metal contamination that has afflicted multiple rivers across northern Thailand since early 2025. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ press release noted that both the Thai and Myanmar representatives agreed to convene a joint working group on the issue “as soon as possible” and that a joint field visit would follow. Sihasak’s visit comes three months after Myanmar and Thailand signed a six-page agreement laying out the terms to jointly monitor the ongoing transboundary water pollution crisis linked to unregulated mining operations in Myanmar. Sources within the Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed to Mongabay that the joint working group born out of this agreement has not met once since the agreement was signed Aug. 6. Even before the delay, the agreement on river pollution monitoring was met with sharp criticism by civil society and government officials who warned that the numerous revisions to the agreement — requested by the Myanmar side and accepted by the Thai side — meant that the bilateral efforts would likely fail to achieve anything meaningful for the…
items.t: Thailand-Myanmar river pollution agreement was weakened, then signed. China remains silent

items.title: Band of baby sea turtles swims into ocean after historic California nesting
items.summary:
Hatchlings emerge after discovery in September of first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on US west coast

Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific.

The eggs incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach after the historic discovery of two separate nests in September at southern California beaches, a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions.

items.t: Band of baby sea turtles swims out to sea after historic California nesting

items.title: Fish pay the price for sacred rituals at Mumbai’s Banganga Tank
items.summary: In October, hundreds of fish were found dead in Mumbai’s Banganga Tank, an ancient freshwater tank considered sacred with roots in Indian mythology. Fish deaths have become nearly an annual occurrence there following the Pitru Paksha rituals, when flowers and various food items are immersed in the water. The immersions likely cause a severe drop in dissolved oxygen levels, killing aquatic life in the tank, experts say. “This has been going on for the last 10 years,” activist Rohit Manohar Joshi, president of Yeoor Environmental Society, told Mongabay. “Every year, fish die because of the rituals performed during Pitru Paksha.” Banganga Tank is a 10-meter- (33-foot-) deep water tank located within the expansive Walkeshwar Temple complex. The water in Banganga Tank is fed by a natural underground freshwater spring below the tank on Mumbai’s Malabar Hill. Every year, several Hindu devotees observe Pitru Paksha during a 15-day period in September-October, when they perform rituals to honor their ancestors. During these rituals, they also immerse flowers and food items, including rice, flour and ghee, into the tank. Media reports have documented fish deaths following the ritual immersions as far back as 2014. In 2025, the city’s municipal corporation (BMC) reportedly removed 10,000 kilograms (22,000 pounds) of dead fish and floral waste. Last year, activists had written to officials seeking the provision of artificial immersion tanks, similar to those set up near beaches during the Ganpati festival, where devotees could immerse their offerings instead of directly polluting the…
items.t: Fish pay the price for sacred rituals at Mumbai’s Banganga Tank

items.title: Pataxó Indigenous people protest the arrest of a female vice-chief in Brazil’s Bahia
items.summary: Pataxó Indigenous people occupied the entrance to the Civil Police station in the city of Eunápolis, in the far south of Brazil’s Bahia state on Nov 12. It was a peaceful protest against the arrest of two Pataxó leaders in the Barra Velha Indigenous Territory. Erilsa Braz dos Santos, known as Uruba Pataxó, vice-chief of Barra Velha Mother Village, and communicator Karen Pataxó were arrested on Nov. 11 on suspicion of drug trafficking in the region. The Pataxó deny the accusations. Karen was released, but Uruba remained in custody and was transferred to a prison in the city of Teixeira de Freitas on Nov. 12, sparking outrage and mobilization among Indigenous people on social media. “This is a political accusation, because she is a leader who defends her people and her territory,” a protester said in a video published on Instagram by the Media and Art Research Center (Nupomar) and Barra Velha Village during the Eunápolis demonstration. Uruba and Karen were detained during Operation Barra Velha, carried out by the Civil and Military Police in Bahia’s Porto Seguro municipality. According to Indigenous leader Dário Pataxó, the imprisonment is intended to silence those who speak out against drug trafficking in the territory. “We know that their intention is to stop the movement. Uruba is one of those on the frontline. They’ve already stopped [Cacique] Suruí, who was president of the Barra Velha Council of Chiefs and is facing proceedings under house arrest. And now they want to stop Uruba,” Dario told…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Pataxó Indigenous people protest the arrest of a female vice-chief in Brazil’s Bahia

items.title: Environmental groups challenge Mexico’s rollback of protections for world’s smallest porpoise
items.summary: MEXICO CITY — Environmental groups are fighting against relaxed fishing regulations in the Gulf of California, where the last of the vaquita, the world’s smallest porpoise, is close to extinction. In October 2026, changes to the regulations dramatically reduced the area where fishing is prohibited in vaquita habitat. In response, several environmental groups have asked a court to halt the changes, arguing that they threaten the last approximately 10 vaquitas (Phocoena sinus) remaining in the world. “The court can stop this rollback before more of the habitat is exposed to deadly nets,” said Aleira Lara Galicia, executive director of Greenpeace Mexico, one of the groups that filed the Nov. 6 injunction request. The Center for Biological Diversity and the Conservation of Marine Mammals of Mexico were also listed as petitioners. The vaquita averages around 1.5 meters (5 feet) long and weighs up to 54 kilograms (120 pounds). It’s endemic to the Gulf of California, also called the Sea of Cortez, where illegal fishing has decimated vaquita populations over the last three decades. The decline is primarily the result of bycatch in gillnets, which hang down vertically in the water and can drown a vaquita when it gets entangled. Many gillnets are illegally set for totoaba (Totoaba macdonaldi), an endangered fish with a swim bladder that sells for thousands of dollars on the black market, primarily in Asia. To protect the vaquita and other marine life, the gulf has a series of layered and overlapping protected areas. A 225-kilometers squared (approximately…This article was…
items.t: Environmental groups challenge Mexico’s rollback of protections for world’s smallest porpoise

items.title: The power of the paddy: Japan looks to rice fields to help mitigate flooding
items.summary: OSAKI, Japan — Osaki, an agricultural community in northeast Japan, has struggled with flooding in recent years. The area was inundated in 2015, 2019 and 2022, when heavy rains breached river embankments. In response, Osaki farmers and local government have installed more than 5,000 small, earthen dams in the rice paddies that surround the community, according to city officials. They say they hope the dams will mitigate flooding by keeping more water contained to the fields. Speaking to Mongabay, Osaki city officials attribute the uptick in floods, in part, to climate change. It’s a pattern seen across Japan, where climate change-fueled heavy rainfall events have increased in frequency and intensity, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency. In response, officials are rethinking their approach to flood control, with increased focus on “green infrastructure” solutions in rice paddies and other agricultural areas. Japan’s agricultural sector is in decline: The average age of a farmer was nearly 70 in 2026 and the country’s rural population is on a steady downward trend. Agricultural land near cities has been converted into suburbs and industrial zones; these low-lying urban areas can be particularly vulnerable to flooding. With declining agricultural land in mind, researchers have been assessing the flood mitigation potential of not only current agricultural land but also abandoned fields. They say that these assessments highlight the importance of understanding site-specific conditions and developing local countermeasures against flooding. “We need to look at the value…
items.t: The power of the paddy: Japan looks to rice fields to help mitigate flooding

items.title: Working in Cape Cod’s waters, he saw an unusual clam. It was the start of an invasion
items.summary:
The unfamiliar mollusk first turned up in this harvester’s haul in 2023. He asked a scientist to identify it, and together they realized they were seeing a potentially harmful, non-native species

  • Send us your climate questions for the next Stateside guest: Bill McKibben

Shellfish harvester Ernie Eldredge is on the hunt for clams, ankle-deep in water amid a landscape that’s almost desert-like in the wake of the receding tide. He runs his rake through fine white sand again and again without hearing the faint “clink” of its tines hitting a shell.

Eldredge just shrugs and moves on to the next spot. These tidal flats, perched on the elbow of Cape Cod in Chatham, Massachusetts, are constantly changing. Recent fall winds have carried a lot more sand into the area, and Eldredge thinks the clams he was finding over the summer may have moved on.

items.t: Working in Cape Cod’s waters, he saw an unusual clam. It was the start of an invasion

items.title: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
items.summary: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.
items.t: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

items.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
items.summary:
Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human

The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

items.title: Country diary: A hard year on the farm, but I can’t help but feel optimistic | Colin Chappell
items.summary:
Brigg, Lincolnshire: As I turn to the autumn jobs, loading crops and checking our machinery, I have to feel that next year will be better

The days are suddenly short, and the mornings have begun to turn much colder, but – strange as it may seem – I’m feeling optimistic. This happens every year around now – I look around and see well-established winter crops full of potential, hedges and edges full of food for the wildlife, and, for now, some money back in the bank, having sold some of the harvest.

The changing colours help – not only the trees but also the yellow and the browns of the soil changing back to green. Farmers have to be the ultimate gamblers, planting a crop with no idea what price we will achieve or what yield will come. We plant and hope.

items.t: Country diary: A hard year on the farm, but I can’t help but feel optimistic | Colin Chappell

items.title: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?
items.summary:
Along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, its intertidal flats host a wealth of marine life and birds. But extraction industries, tourism and fishing are taking their toll

Stand on the coastline at high tide and you look out over unbroken water, with sandy islands rising a few miles offshore. A few hours later and the view across the Wadden Sea has transformed into a maze of deep channels, drying sandbanks, salt marshes and mud flats.

As the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world, this ever-changing habitat stretches hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands and was awarded world heritage status by Unesco in 2009.

Aerial view of the unique features of the Wadden Sea coast. Photograph: Janis Meyer/CWSS

Continue reading...
items.t: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?

items.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
items.summary: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.
items.t: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

items.title: Chickens are great characters, not cowards | Letters
items.summary:
Jo Barlow kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, brave and funny

Whoever deemed chickens synonymous with cowardice obviously didn’t tell my 14-year‑old bantam who took on a hungry Harris hawk and won (Chickens are synonymous with cowardice. Is it time to stick up for our feathered friends?, 11 November).

I kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, unique characters who could be brave, funny, naughty, loving and kind in equal measure.

items.title: The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain | Letters
items.summary:
Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley respond to concerns that the eagles would destroy seabird populations

Your article (Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November) raises important questions, but overlooks a fundamental point: eagles and seabirds coexisted around Britain’s coastline for thousands of years before eagles were driven to extinction through human persecution. Predation and disturbance are therefore not novel ecological pressures, but historically established interactions that have been absent from much of the British landscape for over a century.

There is a danger here of accepting an ecologically impoverished landscape as our conservation baseline. Seabird colonies have existed in the absence of a native apex predator, but that does not necessarily make predator-free conditions either natural or desirable. Restoring eagles is not simply about recovering a charismatic species; it is about restoring lost ecological relationships and processes.

Continue reading...
items.t: The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain | Letters

items.title: Return of the wild oyster: conservationists bring shellfish back from local extinction off Scottish coast
items.summary:
Scientists succeed in breeding wild oysters in Dornoch Firth, near Inverness, from where they disappeared more than 100 years ago

The baby oysters, with their rough cream-coloured shells and ragged edges, are about the size of a 50 pence piece. But off the north-east coast of Scotland, they are proof of a breakthrough in marine conservation.

For the first time in the UK, scientists have succeeded in breeding wild oysters at a site where they had been locally extinct for more than a century, in the Dornoch Firth north of Inverness.

Continue reading...
items.t: Return of the wild oyster: conservationists bring shellfish back from local extinction off Scottish coast

items.title: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins
items.summary: A groundbreaking drone survey has revealed a startling split in the fate of New Zealand's endangered Erect-crested penguins. While one population has remained stable for decades, another has declined by more than 40%, apparently due to a combination of predators, worsening storms, and changing ocean conditions. Even more surprisingly, the tiny Bounty Islands support nearly as many breeding pairs as the Antipodes Islands, despite being 40 times smaller.
items.t: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins

items.title: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago
items.summary: Dinosaurs may have been snacking on seaweed and other ocean foods more than 100 million years ago, according to surprising new evidence hidden in their fossilized teeth. Researchers discovered chemical signatures suggesting that coastal dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals relied partly on nutrients originating in the sea. The findings reveal that marine resources traveled through ancient food chains, supplementing the diets of everything from plant-eating dinosaurs to predators.
items.t: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago

items.title: Lioness Attacks And Ends The Life Of A 19YO After Being Let Out Of Its Cage For A TikTok Video
items.summary:
A TikTok video captured at a private wildlife farm in Lahore, Pakistan, ended in tragedy after a lioness attacked and slayed a 19-year-old farm worker. 

The young man, identified in reports as Talha, was called over to film content with the big cat after a TikToker arrived at the property. 

However, the animal allegedly became uncontrollable after being let out of its cage. 

The teenager was rushed to a private hospital but later passed away from his injuries . 

Police have since arrested the farm’s owner and the content creator as they investigate what happened. 

The incident has also sparked anger online, with one person reminding others that “lions aren’t stage props.” 

A 19-year-old farm worker lost his life after a lioness was let out for a TikTok video 

Sefa Demirtaş/Pexels (not the real image) 

The fatal incident took place at around 5 p.m. on November 11 at a private wildlife farm in Kahna, Lahore. 

According to reports, the 19-year-old employee was working at the property when TikToker Nouman Hassan arrived to film a video with the lioness. 

Hassan, who reportedly has around 928,000 followers on TikTok and 2.5 million on Instagram, is known for posting videos featuring big cats. 

According to a police complaint cited by the BBC , Hassan allegedly asked the farm worker to join him for the video. He then took the lioness out of its cage and began filming. 

Lahore Police 

However, the situation quickly turned dangerous when the animal reportedly became erratic and attacked the teenager. Talha suffered critical injuries and was taken to a…
items.t: Lioness Attacks And Ends The Life Of A 19YO After Being Let Out Of Its Cage For A TikTok Video

items.title: Bristol aims to become UK’s first ‘wetland city’ and reduce flood risk
items.summary:
Five-year project will create wildlife corridors by building wetlands and increase access to green and blue spaces

Bristol could become home to the UK’s first “wetland city” thanks to a charity’s efforts to create vast wildlife corridors that will reduce flood risk and give people more access to green and blue spaces.

The Wildfowl & Wetlands Trust (WWT) said the five-year initiative would include more than 200 projects to restore and create wetlands across the city. These will range from small household rainwater ponds and street-level rain gardens to restoring river habitats, reconnecting rivers with their floodplains, and creating new wetlands.

Continue reading...
items.t: Bristol aims to become UK’s first ‘wetland city’ and reduce flood risk

items.title: ‘An environmental and welfare disaster’: British salmon loses its organic status
items.summary:
This week the Soil Association withdrew certification from organic salmon after 20 years. What went wrong?

The first haul of farmed salmon in Britain was a relatively modest 14 tonnes, produced off the west coast of Scotland near Fort William in 1971.

For Unilever, the vast multinational that pioneered salmon farming, it was a triumph after years of experimenting with how to cage fish, battle against diseases and cope with the wild weather. Unilever had spotted in the 1960s that farming salmon, which until then was caught wild and remained a relative luxury, would create a mass market, lower costs and provide steady profits. By 1976, it had expanded into three Scottish sites producing 116 tonnes of fish each year.
